title: Projects, programmes & portfolios
blurb: Differentiate projects, programmes and portfolios, and say when programme or portfolio management is the right choice.
question: A city council wants to cut carbon from its 8,000 homes. It plans insulation, solar panels and a new tenant advice service, and it also has dozens of unrelated projects competing for the same budget. Which parts should be run as projects, which as a programme, and why does it need portfolio management too?

teach.body: A project is a unique, transient endeavour that delivers outputs. A programme is a unique, transient strategic endeavour that coordinates related projects and business-as-usual (BAU) activities to achieve beneficial change. A portfolio is a collection of projects and programmes managed together to optimise strategic benefits or efficiency. In plain English: a project builds a thing, a programme makes a bigger change happen, and a portfolio makes sure the organisation is doing the right things overall.

teach.caption: The programme groups related work aimed at one strategic change. The portfolio holds everything, related or not, and decides what gets funded.

rows.label: Contains
values: Projects and programmes, related or not

rows.label: Key question
values: Are we doing the right things?

teach.body: Use a programme when the benefits only arrive if several related projects AND changes to BAU land together. Typical signs: projects that depend on each other or share resources and risks; significant change to how people work; a long-term strategic goal. A programme can mix linear projects (a building) with iterative ones (software), coordinating them so the combined outcome is achieved.

Use portfolio management when there are more good ideas than money, people or management attention. Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls projects and programmes in line with strategy and the organisation's capacity to deliver. It balances risk and return, spots duplication, and stops work that no longer fits, so scarce resources go where they create the most strategic value.

teach.caption: The cycle repeats as strategy, funding and capacity change. Stopping a project that no longer fits is a portfolio success, not a failure.

steps.label: Strategy
steps.sub: Where the organisation wants to be

teach.caption: Strategy flows down; benefits flow back up to show the strategic objectives are being met.

teach.text: Exam trap: 'a programme is just a very big project'. No. Size does not decide it. A programme coordinates RELATED projects and BAU change to achieve benefits no single project could deliver alone. A huge one-off build can still be a single project, and a portfolio's projects need not be related at all.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define each: project (outputs), programme (related projects and BAU for benefits), portfolio (collection managed for strategic fit).
Differentiate them on focus, contents and lifespan, giving the reason for each difference.
Describe a situation where programme management is appropriate: interdependent projects, shared benefits, BAU change.
Describe a situation where portfolio management is appropriate: competing demands, limited capacity, need to prioritise.
Link all three to strategic change: strategy drives the portfolio, which shapes programmes and projects.
Projects deliver outputs; programmes deliver outcomes and benefits; portfolios deliver strategic alignment and balance.
A programme coordinates related projects AND BAU activities. It is not simply a big project.
Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls work in line with strategy and capacity to deliver.
Portfolio components do not have to be related to each other.
Stopping work that no longer fits strategy is good portfolio management.

summary: You can now differentiate projects, programmes and portfolios by what they deliver, what they contain and how long they last. You can also describe when programme management and portfolio management are appropriate, and how all three turn strategy into change.

A.q: Which statement BEST describes a programme?
options: A large project with a bigger budget and team
A set of unrelated work ranked for funding
Related projects and BAU change for benefits
The ongoing operations of a business unit
A.why: A programme is a transient strategic endeavour that coordinates related projects and BAU activities to achieve beneficial change.

whyNot.0: Size does not make a programme. A very large one-off build can still be a single project.
whyNot.1: A collection of work, related or not, ranked against strategy describes a portfolio.
whyNot.3: Ongoing operations are business as usual, not a programme.

A.q: What is the PRIMARY focus of portfolio management?
options: Selecting and prioritising the right work
Delivering a single set of outputs on time
Managing one team's detailed work packages
A.why: Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls projects and programmes in line with strategy and capacity to deliver.

whyNot.1: Delivering one set of outputs is the focus of project management.
whyNot.2: Day-to-day operations are business as usual.
whyNot.3: Detailed work packages are managed within a project.

A.q: Complete the statement: projects deliver ___, whereas programmes deliver ___.
A.why: Projects deliver outputs. Programmes coordinate those outputs and BAU change so the outcomes and benefits are achieved.

whyNot.0: This is reversed: projects deliver outputs; programmes are concerned with benefits.
whyNot.1: Strategy is set by the organisation, not delivered by a project.
whyNot.2: This is reversed: outputs come from projects, while programmes focus on outcomes and benefits.

B.q: A water company has 60 proposed projects but only enough money and people for about 20 of them. Which approach is MOST appropriate for deciding which go ahead?
B.why: Choosing between competing proposals with limited capacity, in line with strategy, is exactly what portfolio management is for.

whyNot.0: A programme coordinates related work towards shared benefits; it does not choose between 60 competing ideas.
whyNot.2: Project management delivers approved projects; cost alone is not a sound basis for selection.
whyNot.3: Departments deciding separately would not prioritise across the whole organisation.

B.q: A university is moving its teaching online. It needs a new learning platform, recorded lectures, staff training and new student support processes, and the benefits only appear when all of these are in place. Why is programme management appropriate?
options: The total budget is too big for one project
Each piece of work is unrelated to the others
It removes the need for a sponsor for the work
Related projects and BAU share the benefits
B.why: The projects depend on each other and on BAU changes, and the benefits only come when they all land together: the classic case for a programme.

whyNot.0: Budget size alone does not decide it; the interdependence of the work does.
whyNot.1: The work is closely related, which is why a programme is needed.
whyNot.2: Programmes still need a sponsor; programme management does not remove governance roles.

B.q:
Which TWO are typical reasons for using portfolio management?
1) Limited resources must be shared across competing work
2) A single output needs to be delivered
3) Investment must be balanced against strategy
4) A team needs its daily tasks assigned
B.why: Portfolio management exists to prioritise competing work within limited capacity and to balance investment against strategy.

whyNot.0: Delivering a single output is project management.
whyNot.1: Delivering an output and assigning daily tasks are both project-level activities.
whyNot.3: Balancing investment is right, but daily task assignment belongs to a project team.

C.q: Which question is a portfolio manager MOST concerned with answering?
options: Are we doing the right projects?
Is this project on time and budget?
Is this work package complete yet?
C.why: The portfolio level asks whether the organisation is investing in the right work for its strategy and capacity.

whyNot.1: Time and budget for one project is the project manager's concern.
whyNot.2: Whether a programme's benefits are being realised is the programme's concern.
whyNot.3: Work package completion is tracked within a project.

C.q: Riverside Council's Net Zero Homes programme includes an insulation project, a solar panel project and a new tenant advice service run by the existing housing team. Why is the advice service part of the programme?
options: Programmes may contain only BAU, not projects
Programmes coordinate BAU change, not just projects
It counts as a project because it is in a programme
Every BAU service must sit inside a programme
C.why: A programme coordinates related projects AND business-as-usual activities, because benefits often depend on changes to how BAU works.

whyNot.0: Programmes contain projects too; here there are two.
whyNot.2: Being in a programme does not turn routine BAU work into a project.
whyNot.3: Most BAU services sit outside any programme; only BAU change linked to the programme's benefits is included.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a portfolio?
options: Components are chosen to fit the strategy
Its components need not be related at all
It exists to deliver one set of outputs
C.why: Delivering one set of outputs describes a project. A portfolio is a collection of projects and programmes managed for strategic fit.

whyNot.0: Strategic fit is the main basis for choosing portfolio components.
whyNot.1: This is true: unlike a programme, a portfolio can hold unrelated work.
whyNot.2: This is true: portfolios are managed within the organisation's capacity to deliver.

reteach.title: A family getting ready for a baby
reteach.question: A couple are expecting their first baby. They have one budget for the year and lots of ideas: a new car, a kitchen refit, a holiday, and getting the home ready for the baby. How do projects, a programme and a portfolio show up here?

blocks.body: Decorating the nursery is a project: one clear output, then it is done. 'Be ready for the baby' is a programme: the nursery, fitting a car seat, arranging parental leave and changing the daily routine only deliver the benefit (a calm, safe start) if they all come together. The year's budget, which weighs the baby plans against the kitchen, car and holiday, is the portfolio.

levels.label: Portfolio
levels.sub: This year's budget: baby, car, kitchen, holiday

levels.label: Programme
levels.sub: Ready for the baby: related changes together

blocks.text: Notice the kitchen refit is in the portfolio but not in the baby programme: it is unrelated. Portfolios can hold unrelated work; programmes hold related work aimed at one change.

explain.body: A project delivers a defined set of outputs within agreed time, cost and quality. Its manager's focus is doing the work right: planning, controlling and handing over.

test.q: A project manager's main concern is BEST summarised as which of the following?
test.why: The project manager plans and controls the work to deliver the agreed outputs.

whyNot.0: Choosing what to fund is a portfolio decision.
whyNot.1: Coordinating benefits across related projects is the programme's role.

explain.body: A programme coordinates related projects and BAU change so that their combined outcomes deliver benefits. Use one when the pieces depend on each other and the benefit only comes when they all land.

test.q: Which situation MOST clearly calls for programme management?
options: Several linked projects share one benefit
Monthly reporting to the finance team
test.why: Interdependent projects whose benefit only appears when they combine are the classic case for a programme.

whyNot.1: A self-contained move is a single project.
whyNot.2: Monthly reporting is business as usual.
whyNot.3: Ranking unrelated bids is portfolio management.

explain.body: Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls projects and programmes in line with strategy and the organisation's capacity to deliver. It asks: are we doing the right things, and can we resource them?

explain.caption: An illustrative split of one year's change budget across a portfolio.

test.q: Complete the statement: portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls work in line with strategy and ___.
test.why: Portfolios are managed against both strategy and the organisation's capacity (money, people, attention) to deliver.

whyNot.0: A project schedule is a project-level plan, not the basis for portfolio choices.
whyNot.2: Suppliers do not set an organisation's priorities.
whyNot.3: Individual preferences are exactly what objective portfolio prioritisation avoids.

explain.h: How they connect to strategic change
explain.body: Strategy drives the portfolio. The portfolio shapes and funds programmes and projects. Projects deliver outputs, programmes turn them into benefits, and those benefits show the strategy is being achieved.

test.q: Which sequence best shows how an organisation's strategy becomes change?
options: BAU, then projects, then the strategy
test.why: Strategy sets direction; the portfolio chooses the work; programmes coordinate it; projects deliver the outputs.

whyNot.0: Strategy comes first and drives which projects are chosen, not the reverse.
whyNot.1: BAU absorbs change at the end; it does not set strategy.
whyNot.3: Strategy must come before the programmes it is meant to drive.
